soil-env-081.title: The Sahel, where the Sahara's edge keeps moving
soil-env-081.text: Over the past 50 years the Sahel has lost approximately 650,000 km2 of productive agricultural land. This hot, dry belt gets 100–600 mm of rain a year, and there climate change and human activity combine. Since 1900 the Sahara has reportedly expanded 250 km southward along a 6,000 km west–east front. Lake Chad has shrunk by over 90% since 1987 through irrigation withdrawals and lower rainfall, displacing millions of people. The desert's edge has always moved. The Sahara has swung between wet grassland and dry desert every 20,000 years, linked to a roughly 40,000-year cycle in Earth's axial tilt between 22° and 24.5°.

soil-env-092.title: Deserts that came and went long before people
soil-env-092.text: Beyond the present edges of deserts such as the Sahara lie paleodeserts: large sand seas now held in place by vegetation. Deserts grew and shrank for ages, mostly independently of people. Centuries ago, severe land deterioration in arid regions centred on three densely populated areas: the Mediterranean, the Mesopotamian Valley and China's Loess Plateau. The earliest known discussion followed the French colonization of West Africa, when the Comité d'Etudes commissioned a study of the Sahara's prehistoric spread. The modern study of desertification grew out of research on the Sahel drought of the 1980s.

soil-env-069.title: Farmland bears most of the damage
soil-env-069.text: By 2025, unsustainable farming had degraded 996 Mha of agricultural land, over 60% of all human-induced land degradation. Farmers' local choices shape it, and so do global drivers such as trade, climate change and demographic change. In high-income countries, heavy fertilizer use masks severe per-hectare losses. It brings diminishing returns and can worsen degradation through acidification, nutrient imbalances and pollution. Sub-Saharan Africa shows low yield losses from degradation, mainly because limited access to inputs, machinery, credit and markets dominates its yield gaps. The human cost is stark. In 2025, 47 million stunted children under five lived where stunting overlaps significant yield losses from degradation. Southern Asia and sub-Saharan Africa combine degraded land with high poverty.

soil-env-068.title: How fragile is a landscape? Sensitivity and resilience
soil-env-068.text: A landscape that bends is not the same as one that breaks. Two measures together describe how vulnerable land is to degradation. Sensitivity is the degree to which a land system changes under natural forces, human intervention or both. Resilience is a landscape's ability to absorb change without altering the balance of species in its community, and to return to its original state afterwards. Land-use management can raise or lower resilience. Degraded land is less resilient, so a shock can drive it into further degradation.

soil-env-064.title: The many faces of land degradation
soil-env-064.text: More than 36 types of land degradation can be assessed, and people cause or worsen every one of them. Some have been known for centuries: water, wind and mechanical erosion, and physical, chemical and biological decline. Four types have emerged in the last 50 years. They are pollution, loss of arable land to construction and expansion, artificial radioactivity, and limits on land use from armed conflict. The full list includes contamination, acidification, sheet erosion, silting, aridification, salinization and urbanization.

soil-env-088.title: China's Great Green Wall against the Gobi
soil-env-088.text: Begun in 1978, China's Three-North Shelter Forest Program is planned to finish around 2050 as a barrier about 4,828 km long and up to 1,448 km wide. Its windbreak strips, called shelterbelts, were meant to hold back the Gobi Desert and supply timber. It set out to raise northern China's forest cover from 5 to 15 percent. By 2000, water use, mining, excess farming and wood cutting had desertified 29.7% of China. By 2009 China's planted forest covered more than 500,000 square kilometres, the largest artificial forest in the world. The Gobi grew by 10,000 square kilometres a year in the 1980s but was shrinking by more than 2,000 a year in 2022. In 2024 China finished a 3,000 km green belt around the Taklamakan Desert, and desert cover fell from 27.2% to 26.8% over a decade. Reports credit the program with reversing the Gobi's spread, but critics question tree survival, water use and whether it tackles the causes. A 2023 study found only a fifth of surviving forests became forest stands within 10 years, and a tenth were alive after 40. Dense exotic plantings on the Loess Plateau may worsen water shortages. Monoculture left trees open to disease: in 2000 one billion poplars in Ningxia were lost to a single disease.

soil-env-089.title: Africa's Great Green Wall, from tree line to mosaic
soil-env-089.text: In the 1950s Richard St. Barbe Baker proposed a 'Green front', a 50-kilometre-deep buffer of trees against the expanding desert. The African Union adopted its own version in 2007: a belt of trees across the Sahel from Djibouti to Dakar, 15 km wide and 7,775 km long. The wall grew into a mosaic of water harvesting, protected greenery and improved indigenous land use that helps the ground retain seasonal rainfall. By 2030 it aims to restore 100 million hectares of degraded land, capture 250 million tonnes of carbon dioxide and create 10 million jobs. Progress figures differ widely. A 2020 UNCCD report found only 4% of the planned area covered, while about 18 million hectares were restored by 2023 and about 30 million by 2024. Nigeria has restored 4.9 million hectares and Ethiopia has reclaimed 15 million. Critics question the colonial origins of the word 'desertification', the mostly European funding and top-down strategies that push sedentarization, the settling of mobile herders. Little monitoring has been done. By 2023, terrorist threats, weak political leadership and too little funding put the project at risk of collapse.

soil-env-087.title: Farmer-managed natural regeneration and the underground forest
soil-env-087.text: A field that looks bare may hide an 'underground forest' of living stumps. Each stump can send up 10 to 30 stems, and farmers keep the tallest and straightest. This is farmer-managed natural regeneration, a low-cost way to regrow trees and shrubs from living stumps, roots and seeds. Australian agricultural economist Tony Rinaudo developed it in West Africa in the 1980s, adapting the centuries-old practices of coppicing and pollarding. Trees among crops and pastures raise yields, soil fertility, organic matter and soil moisture, and reduce wind damage and erosion. Pruned residue mulches the fields, raising water retention and cutting evaporation. Faidherbia albida, the 'fertiliser tree', fixes nitrogen, and its falling leaves add nutrients and organic matter. Trials and long-running programs suggest the method can at least double crop yields on low-fertility soils. By 2004 it was practised on over five million hectares, half of Niger's farmland, after nurseries and tree planting had largely failed. One obstacle was legal. From the 1930s until 1993, Niger's forestry laws took tree ownership out of people's hands, until property-law changes eased it.

soil-env-096.title: Overgrazing: when herds eat faster than grass grows
soil-env-096.text: Overgrazing is thought to be the principal cause of grassland decline, and it is one of the farming activities that cause desertification. It happens when animals eat grass faster than it can grow back, as when pastures are stocked above their livestock carrying capacity. Rapid eating and constant trampling stop the grass regrowing. The suppressed sward, the grass cover, then invites rats and insects that hold growth back further. Overgrazing is among the improper farming practices that accelerate soil erosion and degrade land. It is also a main cause of shrubs and bushes spreading into grasslands and savannas. Shrinking farmland makes it worse. Urbanization leaves less land, so farmers pack small plots densely with animals and must still gather much grass for long alpine winters.

soil-env-074.title: How land is stripped bare and turned to desert
soil-env-074.text: Population growth can turn once-acceptable farming into unsustainable overgrazing, over-farming and deforestation. Those human pressures act alongside natural ones. Overgrazing keeps livestock on land for long periods without replanting grass, leaving it bare to harden in the sun and lose nutrients to the wind. Overcultivation and monocropping drain nutrients. The depleted soil loses organic matter and its ability to hold moisture, then hardens and cracks. Intensive farming needs more fertilizer, pesticides and machinery, and continuous use rapidly depletes soil nutrients. Nature works on its own schedule. The Sahara owes its existence to natural changes in solar insolation, the sunlight reaching the ground, caused by Earth's orbital precession. These alter the West African Monsoon and trigger vegetation and dust feedbacks. Regional studies find soil health, human activities and weather all contribute, in different balances. In Shaanxi, meteorological factors work against desertification while the soil worsens it.

soil-env-075.title: Do people make deserts? A long-running dispute
soil-env-075.text: Early studies named overgrazing, the overconsumption of vegetation by livestock, as one of the most common causes of desertification. Today the role of local overexploitation in recent desertification is controversial. The Sahel is the test case. Its drought is now thought to stem mainly from rainfall variability set by sea surface temperatures. Those temperatures are driven by natural variability, sulphate aerosols and greenhouse gases. Changing ocean temperatures and lower sulfate emissions have since re-greened the Sahel. That has led some scholars to call vegetation loss caused by farming a minor factor. Others look further back. Overgrazing by local cattle may have partly driven the mid-Holocene change of the Sahara from savanna to desert. Meanwhile, studies of critical regions confirm that human activities and soil health join meteorological factors as main contributors. The weight of each remains disputed.

soil-env-083.title: South America's spreading dry ground
soil-env-083.text: A quarter of South America is drylands, and over 68% of the continent has suffered soil erosion from deforestation and overgrazing. Between 27 and 43% of the land in Bolivia, Chile, Ecuador and Peru is at risk of desertification. In Argentina, Mexico and Paraguay, more than half the land is degraded by desertification and cannot be farmed. Rural Mexico loses about 1,000 km2 of land a year this way. Drought in Central America has driven unemployment, food insecurity and migration.

soil-env-090.title: Managed grazing and its contested carbon promise
soil-env-090.text: In managed grazing, herds move through many small fenced paddocks every day or two, mimicking natural grazers so the grass can regrow. Restored grasslands store atmospheric CO2 as plant material, whereas confined grazing livestock keep grass growth low. Proponents claim wider use could raise soil carbon across the world's 3.5 billion hectares of agricultural grassland and offset nearly 12 years of CO2 emissions. Many researchers dispute these claims. They say the method neither reverses desertification nor offsets its emissions.

soil-env-095.title: Grassland degradation: brown patches that spread for decades
soil-env-095.text: In China's Tibetan and Inner Mongolian region, 2,460 km2 of grassland is degraded every year. Grassland degradation, also called vegetation or steppe degradation, is a biotic disturbance in which grass struggles to grow or disappears. Overgrazing, burrowing small mammals and climate change are the usual causes. Since the 1970s it has hit alpine meadows and grasslands, notably in that region and in the Philippines. It works slowly. Dead brown patches appear first and, if untreated, spread over many acres across years or decades, and restoration is just as slow. Warming speeds evaporation, and both heavy rain and drought hinder grass. Most sources link the problem to climate change, but some scientists dismiss it as an insignificant cause. Roads, herders' settlements and their animals, monocropping of converted grassland, deforestation and medicinal plant gathering add to the damage. A spiral follows. Less arable land and lower harvests push farmers onto smaller plots that are more easily overgrazed and exhausted, and livestock numbers fall. With fewer plants to anchor the soil, erosion and dust storms increase, and more carbon and nitrogen may escape to the atmosphere. On the Tibetan Plateau 15–20% of species are now endangered, and carbon and nitrogen losses cost $8,033/ha and $13,315/ha respectively. In northern China it affects 400 million people a year, with 54 billion yuan of annual economic loss.

soil-env-207.title: When native shrubs crowd out the grass
soil-env-207.text: About 500 million hectares of grassland, savanna and woodland, on every continent, are filling in with bushes. This is woody plant encroachment: the spread and thickening of native woody plants, bushes and shrubs at the expense of grasses and forbs, the non-woody flowering plants. Encroachers are native, unlike introduced invasive species. They count as encroachers when they outcompete other native species. Encroachment has run at unparalleled rates since the mid-19th century and is classed as a type of grassland degradation. Per decade, rates reach 10-20 percent in North America, 8 percent in South America, 2.4 percent in Africa, and 1 percent in Australia and the Eurasian steppes. Open grassland can become closed woodland. Many treat this as land degradation that harms biodiversity, groundwater recharge, carbon storage and grazing capacity. In North America, each 1 percent increase in woody cover cuts carrying capacity by 0.6 to 1.6 cattle per 100 hectares. Others argue it is natural succession, and its impacts depend on context. In arid lands it has been called 'green desertification', though grass can survive between the canopies, whereas desertification leaves bare soil without organic matter. Soil quality declines under encroachment in arid and semi-arid regions. In Mediterranean and very humid climates it often improves, with more topsoil carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus.

soil-env-206.title: Measuring dryness with the aridity index
soil-env-206.text: A drought ends; aridity stays. Aridity is permanent, whereas drought is temporary. The aridity index puts a number on how dry the climate is at a given place. UNEP's 1992 index compares average annual precipitation with potential evapotranspiration in the same units, so it rises as conditions get wetter. Its classes are hyperarid (below 0.05, 7.5% of land), arid (0.05-0.20, 12.1%), semi-arid (0.20-0.50, 17.7%) and dry subhumid (0.50-0.65, 9.9%). One of the first indices, by Köppen and Geiger, set an annual rainfall threshold that depends on mean annual temperature and the season the rain falls in.

soil-env-094.title: Soil unsealing: prying the pavement off
soil-env-094.text: In the Walloon Region and Germany, new urban projects are offset by removing sealed surfaces elsewhere, under a 'no net land take' principle. Soil unsealing removes asphalt, cement and other human-made covers so a sealed soil can perform its natural functions again. Because sealing losses are mostly irreversible, unsealing is very difficult, and research on it is very limited. Urban, barren or old dumping soils can become parks, green roofs and gardens, but only after thorough decontamination. In a Palermo field trial, vegetated de-sealing stabilised infiltration and raised microbial activity over eighteen months. Crushed asphalt kept higher permeability but less plant cover.

soil-env-205.title: Restoring drylands, one island of plants at a time
soil-env-205.text: Rangelands cover about 25% of drylands, and restoring them counts as a climate mitigation option because of their potential to sequester carbon. Dryland restoration returns degraded drylands to their former function, or manages them so they degrade no further. It is especially hard: rain is rare and variable, temperatures are high, soils are infertile and invasive species spread. One answer is restoration islands, small well-placed plantings that spread into neighbouring ground. They suit patchy dryland vegetation and reduce soil erosion. Soil fauna improve structure, nutrient cycling and infiltration. They can be helped with endemic species, nucleation sites and mulching to keep the soil moist.

soil-env-098.title: Light, moderate, high: grading grassland decline
soil-env-098.text: At its worst, grassland becomes heitutan, 'black beach' or black-soil-land: bare, unusable black soil extending 10–15 cm below ground level. Before that, grassland degradation passes through three stages. Lightly degraded grassland has scattered patches of dead or missing grass. In moderately degraded grassland the patches grow in size and number, plant and animal diversity clearly falls, and pests such as rats and insects damage soil and plants. Highly degraded grassland is a vast expanse of dead grass, fit for neither crops nor livestock, with very low diversity and a few poisonous plants.

soil-env-099.title: Matching the cure to the damage on grassland
soil-env-099.text: Grassland restoration fits the treatment to how badly the land is degraded, and early action makes it easier. Lightly degraded land can be fenced from grazing, fertilized or weeded. Grazing may continue at a lower, monitored intensity, for example by rotating fields seasonally. Moderately degraded land needs reseeding and rodent control, and active brush control, the subject of {{ref:soil-env-211}}, can restore areas invaded by woody plants. Highly degraded land with 30% or more plant cover gets semi-artificial grassland. Worse heitutan land needs artificial grassland, with weed and rodent control, plowing, seeding and fertilizing. Success also needs recognition in policy, standard indicators of degradation, scientific innovation, knowledge transfer and data sharing.

soil-env-097.title: Burrowing small mammals: culprits or bystanders?
soil-env-097.text: Marmots, voles, pikas and zokors are blamed for damaging grassland as their populations grow. Their burrowing and gnawing encourage soil erosion and make it hard for plants to root, leaving grass patchy. Not everyone accepts the charge. Others argue that burrowing recycles soil nutrients and that the population rise simply follows increased grazing. Control, by shooting, sterilizing or low-toxicity poison such as Botulin toxin C, aims to manage these populations rather than wipe them out.

soil-env-211.title: Bush control: thinning shrubs, not erasing them
soil-env-211.text: Bush control works best early, at around 3% shrub cover, and prevention is thought cheaper than treatment. Also called brush management, it is action to manage the density and mix of bushes and shrubs in an area. Encroaching native woody plants are thinned, not eradicated, because they still provide functions such as animal habitat. Measures are preventive, such as suitable stocking rates and rotational grazing. They can also be responsive, such as bush thinning, or maintenance, keeping the thinned density. Waiting is costly: encroached grassland can become a stable state that will not recover without intervention. Method matters too, since chemical control can lose more carbon than mechanical thinning.

soil-env-208.title: Why shrubs are winning against grass
soil-env-208.text: Grasses drink from the topsoil and woody plants from the subsoil. By this two-layer theory, overgrazing the grass lets more water reach the subsoil, where bushes use it. Fire suppression and the loss of wild herbivores also favour woody plants. Global change helps them too. Woody plants with the C3 photosynthetic pathway thrive under high CO2, unlike C4 grasses. When rainfall intensity rises, deep soil water usually increases, which benefits bushes more than grasses. The ground matters as well. Coarse-textured soils promote woody growth and fine-textured soils limit it, while moisture and nutrients make downslope and cooler slopes more prone.

soil-env-209.title: More wood, but not necessarily more carbon
soil-env-209.text: Count only the trunks and branches, and invading shrubs look like a carbon sink. Add the grass and soil organic carbon they replace, and the answer turns uncertain. Several studies find above-ground carbon gains entirely offset by below-ground losses. Soil organic carbon tends to rise under encroachment in dry ecosystems and fall in mesic, moderately moist, ones. In tropical savanna soils most of it comes from grass. A meta-analysis of 142 studies found changes in soil organic carbon (0-50 cm) from -50 to 300 percent, with gains under leguminous shrubs and on sandy soils. Rooting depth increases with encroachment, on average by 38 cm and up to 65 cm.

soil-env-210.title: Thirsty bushes and the rain that never reaches the soil
soil-env-210.text: In South Africa, woody canopies catch and evaporate about 44% of rainfall, and up to 10% less rain enters the soil. Bushes use far more rainwater than grasses, so their spread reduces groundwater recharge and alters streamflow. Denser canopies raise transpiration and the evaporation of soil moisture, and enhanced soil porosity can speed soil drought. In arid and semi-arid lands, encroachment reduces stream flows, while woody plant control can improve the connectivity of water resources.

soil-env-071.title: Land degradation neutrality: a target for 2030
soil-env-071.text: By 2030, the world is meant to become land degradation-neutral. Land degradation neutrality is the policy goal behind that date, set in UN Sustainable Development Goal 15. Target 15.3 calls for combating desertification and restoring degraded land and soil, including land hit by desertification, drought and floods. It asks the world to strive for a land degradation-neutral world. Money followed. The Land Degradation Neutrality Fund, launched at UNCCD COP 13 in 2017, invests in projects with environmental, socio-economic and financial returns. It was initially capitalized at US$100 million and is expected to grow to US$300 million. The European Investment Bank agreed to invest up to $45 million. Supporting the goal is one objective of the UNCCD's 2018–2030 Strategic Framework.

reviews.degradation-and-desertification: Soil can slide backward, from a stable climax toward bare rock, and land degradation spreads that loss across a quarter or more of the world's land and billions of people. Most of the drivers are human, from tillage, overgrazing and monocultures to sealing and land consumption, and a warming climate makes them worse while it enlarges the drylands. In those drylands the end point is desertification, with its dust storms, hunger, poverty and migration, though how much people rather than climate drive it is still disputed. Grasslands show the same pattern, losing grass to overgrazing, burrowing mammals and encroaching shrubs. Against all this stand sustainable land management, tree belts, farmer-managed regeneration and the UNCCD's goal of land degradation neutrality, with results that are real but often contested.
